items.title: 6.1.5 Equations of Circles Determined by Given Conditions

source_refs.note: Book p. 168-172: Cases 1-4 (three points; two points and centre on a line; two points and tangent; two points and touching a line); Examples 5-9; Figures 6.5, 6.6; Do You Know? box; determinant box

blocks.text: The general equation of a circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\) contains three independent constants \(g\), \(f\) and \(c\). These can be determined if the equation satisfies three given conditions. We will discuss four different cases.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A circle needs exactly three numbers (\(g\), \(f\), \(c\); or centre \(h\), \(k\) and radius \(r\)), so it needs three independent conditions. Each piece of information gives one equation:
a point on the circle gives one equation; a centre on a given line gives one equation; touching a line gives one equation (distance from centre = radius).

blocks.caption: Our summary of the four cases (not printed in the book)
rows: each point satisfies the general form
two points, centre on a given line
two points + centre satisfies the line
two points, tangent at one of them
two points + normal at the contact point passes through the centre
two points, touching a given line
centre equidistant from the points + distance to the line = radius

blocks.text: Case-1: A Circle Passing through Three Non-collinear Points
If three non-collinear points through which a circle passes are given, we can find the three independent constants \(g\), \(f\) and \(c\) in the general equation.

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: Find the equation of the circle passing through the points \((-3, 3)\), \((-1, 5)\) and \((5, 1)\).
steps:
Given: the circle passes through \((-3, 3)\), \((-1, 5)\) and \((5, 1)\).
To find: its equation.
Method: Case 1. Take the general form (A); each point gives one equation in \(g, f, c\); three points give three equations for three unknowns.

Step 1: Let the equation be
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 \quad \text{...(A)}\]
Why: centre and radius are unknown, and the general form has exactly three constants to fit the three points.

Step 2: Through \((-3, 3)\)
\[(-3)^{2} + (3)^{2} + 2g(-3) + 2f(3) + c = 0\]
\[9 + 9 - 6g + 6f + c = 0\]
\[-6g + 6f + c + 18 = 0 \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: a point lies on a curve exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.

Step 5: Subtract (2) from (1)
\[(-6g + 6f + c + 18)\]
\[- (-2g + 10f + c + 26) = 0\]
\[-6g + 6f + c + 18\]
\[+ 2g - 10f - c - 26 = 0\]
\[-4g - 4f - 8 = 0\]
\[g + f + 2 = 0 \quad \text{...(4)}\]
Why: \(c\) has the same coefficient in every equation, so subtracting removes it; dividing by \(-4\) simplifies.

Step 6: Subtract (3) from (2)
\[(-2g + 10f + c + 26)\]
\[- (10g + 2f + c + 26) = 0\]
\[-2g + 10f + c + 26\]
\[- 10g - 2f - c - 26 = 0\]
\[-12g + 8f = 0\]
\[3g - 2f = 0 \quad \text{...(5)}\]
Why: again \(c\) cancels; dividing by \(-4\) gives (5). Now (4) and (5) are two equations in \(g\) and \(f\) only.

Step 7: Solve for \(f\)
\[\text{From (4): } g = -f - 2\]
\[3(-f - 2) - 2f = 0\]
\[-3f - 6 - 2f = 0\]
\[-5f = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; f = -\dfrac{6}{5}\]
Why: substitution turns two equations into one equation in \(f\).

Step 8: Find \(g\)
\[3g - 2\left(-\dfrac{6}{5}\right) = 0\]
\[3g = -\dfrac{12}{5} \;\Rightarrow\; g = -\dfrac{4}{5}\]
Why: put \(f\) into (5).

Step 9: Find \(c\) from (1)
\[-6\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right) + 6\left(-\dfrac{6}{5}\right)\]
\[+ c + 18 = 0\]
\[\dfrac{24}{5} - \dfrac{36}{5} + c + 18 = 0\]
\[-\dfrac{12}{5} + c + 18 = 0\]
\[c = \dfrac{12}{5} - 18 = -\dfrac{78}{5}\]
Why: any of (1), (2), (3) gives \(c\) once \(g\) and \(f\) are known.

Step 10: Substitute in (A)
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)x\]
\[+ 2\left(-\dfrac{6}{5}\right)y - \dfrac{78}{5} = 0\]
Multiplying both sides by 5:
\[5x^{2} + 5y^{2} - 8x - 12y - 78 = 0\]
Why: a whole-number form is neater and is the book's final answer.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: Infinitely many circles can pass through two points, but exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The box prints the three points as \((x, y)\), \((x_{2}, y_{2})\) and \((x_{3}, y_{3})\). The first given point should be \((x_{1}, y_{1})\), as in the second row of the determinant; \((x, y)\) is the general point of the circle in the first row.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does the determinant work? Expanding it along the first row gives \(k(x^{2} + y^{2}) + (\dots)x + (\dots)y + (\dots) = 0\): a circle (or a line if \(k = 0\), which happens only for collinear points). If \((x, y)\) is one of the three given points, two rows are equal and the determinant is 0, so all three points lie on it.
For Example 5 the determinant works out to \(-4(5x^{2} + 5y^{2} - 8x - 12y - 78) = 0\): the same circle.
Case-2: A Circle Passing through Two Points and Having its Centre on a Given Line

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: A circle with its centre on \(y\)-axis passes through the origin and the point \((a, b)\). Find its equation.
steps:
Given: centre on the \(y\)-axis; the circle passes through \(O(0, 0)\) and \((a, b)\).
To find: its equation.
Method: a centre on the \(y\)-axis has \(x\)-coordinate 0. Since the circle passes through the origin, the distance from the centre to the origin is the radius, so (as in the book) the centre is \((0, r)\). The second point gives an equation for \(r\).

Step 1: Distance from the centre to (a, b) equals r
\[r = \sqrt{(a - 0)^{2} + (b - r)^{2}}\]
Why: every point of the circle is at distance \(r\) from the centre \((0, r)\).

Step 2: Square both sides and simplify
\[r^{2} = a^{2} + (b - r)^{2}\]
\[r^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} - 2br + r^{2}\]
\[2br = a^{2} + b^{2}\]
\[r = \dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2b}, \quad b \ne 0\]
Why: \(r^{2}\) appears on both sides and cancels, leaving a linear equation in \(r\). We need \(b \ne 0\) to divide.

Step 3: Equation with centre (0, r) and radius r
\[(x - 0)^{2} + (y - r)^{2} = r^{2}\]
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 2yr + r^{2} = r^{2}\]
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 2yr = 0\]
Why: standard form; the \(r^{2}\) terms cancel again.

Step 4: Substitute r and clear the fraction
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 2y\left(\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2b}\right) = 0\]
\[b(x^{2} + y^{2}) - (a^{2} + b^{2})y = 0\]
Why: multiplying through by \(b\) removes the denominator (the 2s cancel first).

Check:
\[(0, 0):\; b(0) - (a^{2} + b^{2})(0) = 0\]
\[(a, b):\; b(a^{2} + b^{2}) - (a^{2} + b^{2})b = 0\]
Both points satisfy the equation, and the centre \(\left(0, \frac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2b}\right)\) is on the \(y\)-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book calls the centre \((0, r)\). This assumes the centre is above the origin (\(b > 0\)). If \(b < 0\), the formula gives a negative value: the centre is \(\left(0, \frac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2b}\right)\) below the origin, and the radius is the absolute value \(\frac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2|b|}\). The final equation is the same in both cases.
Here the 'given line' of Case 2 is the \(y\)-axis \(x = 0\), and the two points are \((0, 0)\) and \((a, b)\).
Case 3: A Circle Passing through Two Points and having Tangent at One of These Points

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem: Find the equation of the circle passing through \((1, 2)\) and touching the line \(x - 2y + 4 = 0\) at \((2, 3)\).
steps:
Given: the circle passes through \((1, 2)\) and touches the line \(x - 2y + 4 = 0\) at \((2, 3)\).
To find: its equation.
Method: general form (A). Two conditions come from the points \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 3)\) (the point of contact is on the circle). The third comes from the tangent: the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent, so the normal at \((2, 3)\) passes through the centre \((-g, -f)\).

Step 1: Let the equation be
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 \quad \text{...(A)}\]
Why: three unknowns, three conditions.

Step 2: Through \((1, 2)\)
\[1^{2} + 2^{2} + 2g(1) + 2f(2) + c = 0\]
\[2g + 4f + c + 5 = 0 \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: the point satisfies (A).

Step 3: Through \((2, 3)\)
\[2^{2} + 3^{2} + 2g(2) + 2f(3) + c = 0\]
\[4g + 6f + c + 13 = 0 \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: the point of contact lies on the circle.

Step 4: Slope of the tangent and of the normal
\[x - 2y + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{1}{2}x + 2\]
\[\text{slope of line} = \tfrac{1}{2}\]
\[\text{slope of normal} = -2\]
Why: perpendicular slopes multiply to \(-1\): \(\frac{1}{2} \times (-2) = -1\).

Step 5: Equation of the normal at (2, 3)
\[y - 3 = -2(x - 2)\]
\[y - 3 = -2x + 4\]
\[2x + y - 7 = 0\]
Why: point-slope form through (2, 3) with slope -2.

Step 6: The centre lies on the normal
\[2(-g) + (-f) - 7 = 0\]
\[2g + f = -7 \quad \text{...(3)}\]
Why: the radius to the point of contact lies along the normal, so the centre \((-g, -f)\) satisfies the normal's equation; multiply by \(-1\).

Step 7: Subtract (2) from (1)
\[[2g + 4f + c + 5]\]
\[- [4g + 6f + c + 13] = 0\]
\[-2g - 2f - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow g + f = -4\]
\[f = -4 - g \quad \text{...(4)}\]
Why: \(c\) cancels; we get \(f\) in terms of \(g\).

Step 8: Substituting the value of f in (3) (the book prints "Subtracting value of f in (3)")
\[2g + (-4 - g) = -7\]
\[2g - 4 - g = -7 \Rightarrow g = -3\]
Why: (3) and (4) together leave one unknown.

Step 9: f and c
\[\text{From (4): } f = -4 - (-3) = -1\]
\[\text{In (1): } 2(-3) + 4(-1) + c + 5 = 0\]
\[-6 - 4 + c + 5 = 0 \Rightarrow c = 5\]
Why: back-substitution.

Step 10: Substitute g, f, c in (A)
The book's wording here is garbled: "Thus, the required substiting the values of f, gernd c is equation (A)". It means: substituting the values of g, f and c in equation (A), the required equation of the circle is
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2(-3)x + 2(-1)y + 5 = 0\]
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 6x - 2y + 5 = 0\]
Why: this gives the required circle.

Check:
\[(1, 2):\; 1 + 4 - 6 - 4 + 5 = 0\]
\[(2, 3):\; 4 + 9 - 12 - 6 + 5 = 0\]
Centre \((3, 1)\), radius \(\sqrt{9 + 1 - 5} = \sqrt{5}\). Distance from \((3, 1)\) to the line:
\[\dfrac{|3 - 2(1) + 4|}{\sqrt{1 + 4}} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{5}\]
It equals the radius, so the line is indeed a tangent.
book_errors: Thus, the required substiting the values of f, gernd c is equation (A)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In Example 7 the book prints "Subtracting value of f in (3)"; it should read "Substituting the value of f in (3)".
Its last lines are garbled ("Thus, the required substiting the values of f, gernd c is equation (A) ..."). They should read: "Substituting the values of g, f and c in equation (A), the required equation of the circle is \(x^{2} + y^{2} - 6x - 2y + 5 = 0\)." The book's final answer is correct.
Case 4: A Circle Passing through Two Points and Touching a Given Line

blocks.title: Example 8
blocks.problem: Find the equations of the circles passing through the points \(A(3, 4)\) and \(B(3, -4)\) and touching the line \(x + 2y + 9 = 0\).
steps:
Given: the circles pass through \(A(3, 4)\) and \(B(3, -4)\) and touch the line \(x + 2y + 9 = 0\).
To find: their equations.
Method: (i) the centre is equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\); (ii) a line touches a circle exactly when its perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius.

Step 1: Equal distances to A and B
Let \(O(h, k)\) be the centre (here \(O\) is the centre, not the origin).
\[|\overline{OA}|^{2} = |\overline{OB}|^{2}\]
\[(h - 3)^{2} + (k - 4)^{2}\]
\[= (h - 3)^{2} + (k + 4)^{2}\]
Why: both distances are radii; squaring avoids square roots.

Step 2: Solve for k
\[(k - 4)^{2} = (k + 4)^{2}\]
\[k^{2} - 8k + 16 = k^{2} + 8k + 16\]
\[-8k = 8k \Rightarrow 16k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 0\]
Why: \((h - 3)^{2}\) is on both sides and cancels. So the centre is \((h, 0)\): it lies on the \(x\)-axis, the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\).

Step 3: The radius
\[r = |\overline{OA}| = \sqrt{(h - 3)^{2} + (0 - 4)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{(h - 3)^{2} + 16}\]
Why: distance formula from (h, 0) to A.

Step 4: Distance from the centre to the line
\[\dfrac{|h + 2(0) + 9|}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 2^{2}}} = \dfrac{|h + 9|}{\sqrt{5}}\]
Why: perpendicular distance from \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) to \(ax + by + c = 0\) is \(\frac{|ax_{1} + by_{1} + c|}{\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}}\).

Step 5: Tangency: distance = radius, then square
\[\dfrac{|h + 9|}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{(h - 3)^{2} + 16}\]
\[\dfrac{(h + 9)^{2}}{5} = (h - 3)^{2} + 16\]
\[(h + 9)^{2} = 5[(h - 3)^{2} + 16]\]
Why: the circle touches the line; both sides are non-negative, so squaring loses nothing.

Step 6: Expand and simplify
\[h^{2} + 18h + 81 = 5(h^{2} - 6h + 9 + 16)\]
\[= 5(h^{2} - 6h + 25)\]
\[= 5h^{2} - 30h + 125\]
\[0 = 4h^{2} - 48h + 44\]
\[h^{2} - 12h + 11 = 0\]
Why: bring everything to one side and divide by 4.

Step 7: Factorise
\[h^{2} - 11h - h + 11 = 0\]
\[h(h - 11) - 1(h - 11) = 0\]
\[(h - 11)(h - 1) = 0\]
\[h = 1, \quad h = 11\]
Why: split \(-12h\) as \(-11h - h\) (product 11, sum \(-12\)). Two values of \(h\) mean two circles.

Step 8: Centres and radii
\[\text{centres } (1, 0) \text{ and } (11, 0)\]
\[r_{1} = \sqrt{(1 - 3)^{2} + 16}\]
\[= \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20}\]
\[r_{2} = \sqrt{(11 - 3)^{2} + 16}\]
\[= \sqrt{64 + 16} = \sqrt{80}\]
Why: put each h in the radius formula of Step 3.

Check:
\[\dfrac{|1 + 9|}{\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{5}}\]
\[= 2\sqrt{5} = \sqrt{20}\]
\[\dfrac{|11 + 9|}{\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{5}}\]
\[= 4\sqrt{5} = \sqrt{80}\]
Each distance equals the radius, and \((3, \pm 4)\) satisfy both equations: \(4 + 16 = 20\), \(64 + 16 = 80\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Two answers are natural in Case 4: through two points there is a whole family of circles (centres on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\)), and in general two members of this family touch a given line, one on each side. The quadratic in \(h\) shows this.

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.problem: Find the equation of the circle which touches the \(y\)-axis at a distance of 3 units from the origin and cuts off an intercept of 8 units on the \(x\)-axis.
steps:
Given: the circle touches the \(y\)-axis at a point 3 units from the origin, i.e. at \((0, 3)\) or \((0, -3)\); it cuts a chord of length 8 on the \(x\)-axis.
To find: its equation (all such circles).
Method: a circle touching the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 3)\) has its centre on the horizontal line \(y = 3\), at distance \(r\) from the \(y\)-axis. The \(x\)-intercept is the distance between the roots of the equation obtained by putting \(y = 0\).

Step 1: Locate the centre
Let the point of tangency be \((0, 3)\). The radius to it is perpendicular to the \(y\)-axis (horizontal), so the centre lies on \(y = 3\) and its \(x\)-coordinate is \(\pm r\). Take the centre to the right of the \(y\)-axis:
\[C = (r, 3), \quad \text{radius } r\]
Why: tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

Step 2: Equation of the circle
\[(x - r)^{2} + (y - 3)^{2} = r^{2}\]
\[(x^{2} - 2rx + r^{2}) + (y^{2} - 6y + 9) = r^{2}\]
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 2rx - 6y + 9 = 0\]
Why: standard form, then the \(r^{2}\) terms cancel.

Step 3: Meet the \(x\)-axis
For the intercept on the \(x\)-axis, set \(y = 0\):
\[x^{2} - 2rx + 9 = 0\]
\[x_{1} + x_{2} = 2r, \quad x_{1}x_{2} = 9\]
Why: the roots \(x_{1}, x_{2}\) are where the circle cuts the \(x\)-axis; sum of roots \(= -\frac{b}{a}\), product \(= \frac{c}{a}\).

Step 4: Length of the intercept
\[|x_{1} - x_{2}| = \sqrt{(x_{1} + x_{2})^{2} - 4x_{1}x_{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{4r^{2} - 36}\]
Why: \((x_{1} - x_{2})^{2} = (x_{1} + x_{2})^{2} - 4x_{1}x_{2}\), so we need only the sum and product.

Step 5: Use the given intercept 8
\[\sqrt{4r^{2} - 36} = 8\]
\[4r^{2} - 36 = 64\]
\[4r^{2} = 100 \Rightarrow r^{2} = 25 \Rightarrow r = 5\]
Why: square both sides; the radius is positive, so r = 5.

Step 6: One circle
\[(x - 5)^{2} + (y - 3)^{2} = 25\]
Why: centre (5, 3), radius 5.

Step 7: All four circles by symmetry
The centre may also be left of the \(y\)-axis, and the tangency may be at \((0, -3)\). This gives centres \((\pm 5, \pm 3)\):
\[(x \pm 5)^{2} + (y \pm 3)^{2} = 25\]
Why: the same working with \(-r\) or \(-3\) changes only signs. The \(\pm\) signs are independent (Figure 6.6).

Check:
\[y = 0:\; (x - 5)^{2} + 9 = 25\]
\[(x - 5)^{2} = 16 \Rightarrow x = 1, 9\]
Intercept \(9 - 1 = 8\). On \(x = 0\): \(25 + (y - 3)^{2} = 25\) gives only \(y = 3\), so the circle touches the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 3)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A circle has three constants, so three conditions fix it.
2. Point on the circle: substitute it in the general form.
3. Tangent at a point: the normal there passes through the centre \((-g, -f)\).
4. Touching a line: perpendicular distance from the centre = radius.
5. Touching the \(y\)-axis at \((0, k)\): centre \((\pm r, k)\); touching the \(x\)-axis at \((h, 0)\): centre \((h, \pm r)\).
6. Chord on the \(x\)-axis: put \(y = 0\); length \(= |x_{1} - x_{2}| = \sqrt{(x_{1} + x_{2})^{2} - 4x_{1}x_{2}}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Sign slips when substituting negative coordinates: \((-3)^{2} = 9\) but \(2g(-3) = -6g\).
2. Forgetting that the point of contact is also on the circle (Example 7 uses it twice: on the circle and on the normal).
3. Giving only one circle when the conditions allow two (Example 8) or four (Example 9).
4. Dropping the modulus in the distance formula and then losing a solution.
